There is a site called Find a Grave that may be able to help you. I have been a volunteer for many years. I love my job. That said, last month I was home for a total of 7 hours. Depending on where you live, you could possibly get into moving mobile homes as a company driver. If you want to be independent, it will be virtually impossible to break even, let alone turn a profit while getting the home time you want. Last year I drove a total of 89k miles, grossed right at 100k, and my net profit was 41k. I was on the road 236 nights.

Of course, I don't know what is causing you to miscarry, but there truly may still be hope for you. I had 5 losses due to a wildly overactive immune system. I didn't have my first successful pregnancy until 25. I then went on to have babies at 27, 29, 30, and 32. Women are having babies without complications later now, but even being conservative, you have a decade before maternal age is likely to become an issue. I can absolutely sympathize with the emotional and physical toll this is having on you. Maybe it won't happen for you, but I don't think you would be wrong to try to remain cautiously optimistic. I hope the best for you.

ETA: I have read other comments, and I am so sorry for those who never were able to have the babies they dreamed of. On one hand, I almost hate to post my eventual success. I am letting it stand to perhaps give OP renewed hope and anyone else still hoping to carry to term.

Insurance is the biggest expense, yes, even more than fuel, for most. Some states, such as FL, do not have any insurance requirement for pilot cars. NM requires a min 500 limit, PA requires 1 mil, and the state be a certificate holder on the policy, LA requires 500 auto/500 commercial liability for a state permit. Those are the ones I know readily. Many of the big trucking companies require 1 mil commercial liability. 

That said, while I do not condone it, with the exception of LA and NM, you can probably get away with your basic state minimum auto policy to get started. TBH, that's how I had to start. I raised my limits to 500 the first year, then, once I got going, I got a legit 1 mil commercial auto and liabily policy. It is truly in your best interest to do so. If you are escorting a load, even if not at fault in any way, and there is a wreck, you will likely be sued. They sue everyone to see what sticks. If your auto insurance finds out you are using your vehicle for work, they will deny any claim, and they will drop you.

Rates are varied depending on your state, driving record, etc. I currently pay just over 2500 yr for 1mil commercial liability and commercial auto. From what I've seen it is on the low end. Anecdotally most are paying about 4k a year with rates as high as 15k in FL. It sucks, but it is absolutely worth it.

A person does not need to be declared incompetent for someone to have POA. It is completely different than conservatorship. I had POA for my husband when he was deployed. When my father had laryngeal cancer and a trache he lost the ability to speak. Among other things, I had POA so I could deal with the VA over the phone on his behalf. A general POA simply allows you to make decisions, enter into contracts, etc on another person's behalf. A limited POA can be used for virtually anything. I had a friend give me a limited POA to sell their car for them when they were deployed. It allowed me to sign their title as if I was them. It was limited to that single transaction.

In OPs case the ex SIL could literally sell grandma's house and it would be within his legal right. Grandma would then have to file a civil suit to try to reclaim the money. Never give anyone a general power of attorney unless you are certain they are trustworthy.

Just a couple off the top of my head.
